analysis.one_liner: Bans price gouging on oil and other essential goods during declared national emergencies.
analysis.headline: Despite 58 cosponsors including 9 Republicans, the bill died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the President declare a national economic emergency when the price or supply of essentials like gasoline, heating oil, or propane suddenly spikes. During the emergency, selling those goods above the seller's actual costs plus a reasonable profit would be a crime, punishable by up to 5 years in prison, a $500,000 fine, and surrender of all the profits, and the Justice Department or any state could sue for double damages. Congress could end an emergency by passing a joint resolution, and courts could review the President's declaration.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy gasoline, home heating oil, propane, and other essentials during a crisis — for example, drivers and homeowners hit by an oil price spike after a war or supply shock. The bill would bar sellers from charging prices beyond their actual costs plus a reasonable profit during such an emergency, and would let the government claw back excess profits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of gasoline and heating oil

how_it_helps.text: During a declared national economic emergency, sellers could not charge an 'excessive price' — one above the seller's actual costs plus a reasonable profit — on essentials like crude oil, gasoline, diesel, home heating oil, and propane.
Knowingly violating the ban would carry up to 5 years in prison, a fine of up to $500,000, and mandatory disgorgement of all profits earned on the affected commodities.
The Justice Department and state governments could sue violators in federal court for injunctions, restitution, and double the profits earned from profiteering.

The bill included checks on the emergency power itself: an emergency would lapse after 180 days unless extended, Congress could terminate it (or the covered commodities) by joint resolution, and the President's determination would be subject to court review.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel distributors and retailers, who would face criminal exposure, confiscation of profits, and double damages in civil suits for selling above cost-plus-a-reasonable-profit during a declared emergency. Other suppliers of commodities the President designates as essential would bear the same risk.

drawbacks.text: The pricing standard is a cost-plus cap: sellers could earn only a 'reasonable profit' over actual costs, and no allowance would be made for replacement costs if the seller expects to recoup them later. Sellers who might otherwise rush in extra supply during a shortage could hold back, since the law penalizes the very price signals that draw supply in — a standard criticism of anti-gouging rules.

The bill gives the President sweeping discretion to declare an emergency and designate any commodity he deems important, with court review so deferential (clear and convincing evidence of arbitrary action) that it would rarely block a declaration; extensions of the 180-day emergency could be renewed every 90 days with no limit, and Congress's termination power requires passing a joint resolution, which a hostile chamber or a presidential veto could defeat.

The bill would do nothing about high prices in ordinary times — its protections apply only after the President formally declares an emergency, so a price spike would remain legal unless and until that declaration came.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the bill offered real protection against exactly the scenario then unfolding: introduced in September 1990, weeks after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait sent oil and gasoline prices jumping, it would have made crisis-driven profiteering on fuel a crime with teeth (prison, fines, profit disgorgement, double damages) and let states sue alongside the federal government. The cost is real but narrower: a cost-plus price ceiling is a blunt tool that can discourage sellers from adding supply precisely when shortages bite, and the emergency trigger hands the President broad, hard-to-review power. On balance the design is defensible — the emergency is time-limited, Congress can terminate it, and it leaves ordinary market pricing alone — but the cap would have been hard to apply to complex fuel supply chains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Criminal Justice Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dick Durbin introduced the bill on September 11, 1990, with 27 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day.
On October 2, 1990, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Criminal Justice — the last action ever taken on it.
It attracted 58 cosponsors, including 9 Republicans, but the committee never reported it, and no vote was ever held before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum producers, refiners, and fuel sellers — they faced no new liability, no profit disgorgement, and no price limits during the 1990-91 oil price spike, because the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

for.name: Rep. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Emergency Anti-Profiteering Act of 1990 to criminalize profiteering on essential commodities during declared emergencies.

for.name: 49 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 27 original cosponsors named at introduction.

for.name: 9 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Gunderson, Shays, and Pease.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jack Brooks)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 11, 1990, and never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it was sent to the Criminal Justice Subcommittee on October 2 and no further action followed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 58 cosponsors, 9 of them Republicans out of 175 House Republicans — but no vote ever occurred, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.industry: Oil and petroleum industry (producers, refiners, distributors, retailers)
industries.note: The bill was aimed squarely at this industry: during a declared emergency, selling crude oil, gasoline, diesel, or heating oil above actual costs plus a reasonable profit would become a crime carrying prison time, a $500,000 fine, surrender of all profits, and double damages in civil suits. The industry's ability to profit from crisis-driven price spikes is exactly what the bill would have taken away, and that same spike is what consumers pay for at the pump.

industries.industry: Suppliers of other presidentially designated essential commodities
industries.note: The President could designate any commodity important to the economy or to public health and safety as an 'essential commodity', extending the same cost-plus pricing ban and penalties to that supplier. Their interest in charging market-clearing prices during a disruption runs against the consumers the bill would protect.
